This directly aligns with reform bail using risk assessment tools rather than monetary conditions.

She supported Proposition 36 (2024), which reinstated criminal penalties for repeat drug/theft offenders, stating it "will reinstate accountability on crimes destroying the quality of life." She was critical of Prop 47's elimination of drug courts and rehabilitation incentives.

rows.name: Lindsey P. Horvath
rows.prior_reasoning: Horvath explicitly stated in 2025: 'In 2020, the people of Los Angeles County overwhelmingly approved Measure J to shift County resources away from incarceration and toward community-based investments.' She championed closure of Men's Central Jail, led juvenile justice transformation away from the Probation Department toward a youth development model, and opposed the Grants Pass ruling that 'green lights the criminalization of homelessness and poverty.' Her 2024-25 budget directed 28 positions to youth justice reform and 10 positions to jail closure implementation.

rows.name: Lori Trahan
rows.prior_reasoning: Trahan supports rehabilitation and treatment over incarceration for nonviolent drug offenses, co-sponsored federal death penalty abolition, and backed reducing prosecutorial use of mandatory minimums. Her record reflects diverting prosecutorial resources away from low-level drug offenses toward violent crime prevention.

rows.name: Marjorie C. Decker
rows.prior_reasoning: Decker co-sponsored Overdose Prevention Centers (treating drug use as a health matter rather than criminal) and Age of Criminal Majority to 21 (diversion over prosecution for young adults), reflecting a framework where connection to treatment and services is preferred over a criminal record.

rows.name: Michael E. Verveer

rows.name: Patricia D. Jehlen

rows.name: Richard Neal

His CURE rating (78%) and First Step Act support reflect a prosecution philosophy emphasizing diversion and treatment over incarceration.

rows.name: Richelle Andrae

rows.name: Sal N. DiDomenico

rows.name: Seth Moulton
rows.prior_reasoning: Moulton supports legalizing marijuana and reducing drug-based convictions, and backs diversion programs over incarceration for non-violent offenses. His criminal justice philosophy consistently prioritizes alternatives to prosecution and rehabilitation for non-violent cases.

rows.name: William C. Smith, Jr.
rows.prior_reasoning: Smith has used the Judicial Proceedings chair role to prioritize balanced prosecution approaches, supporting reforms to reduce mass incarceration while maintaining public safety.

rows.name: William N. Brownsberger
rows.prior_reasoning: Criminal justice work consistently emphasizes diversion over prosecution: supported pretrial services, expanded alternatives to incarceration, and argued mandatory minimum sentences cause disproportionate harm. Harm reduction advocacy including supervised injection facilities and marijuana legalization reflects a framework where prosecution is a last resort.

kept.name: Angie Christides
kept.prior_reasoning: Christides says bail decisions should be "based on minimizing the risk to public safety and the individual circumstances." This is balanced — public safety is a primary consideration alongside individualized review. Neither strongly skeptical of prosecution nor deferential to it; aligns with stance 3: treat both sides equally.

kept.name: Donna Tryfman
kept.prior_reasoning: Tryfman states: "Pretrial custody decisions should not be based on punishment. Every person is presumed innocent." She explicitly rejects punishment as a rationale for pretrial detention, indicating a skeptical posture toward detention requests — while not signaling hostility to prosecution generally.

kept.name: Irene Lee
kept.prior_reasoning: Lee says cash bail "must reflect actual ability to pay" and her primary bail questions are: "Is this person a danger? Are they likely to come back to court?" She focuses on flight risk and public safety rather than deferring to prosecution recommendations, aligning with stance 2: skeptical, holds prosecution to strict standards.

kept.name: Patrick Connolly
kept.prior_reasoning: Connolly cites "releasing defendants appropriately under current law" as a point of pride, indicating he follows statutory guidance on pretrial detention rather than reflexively trusting or distrusting prosecutors. Aligns with stance 3: treat both sides equally, let the process work.

kept.name: Paul A. Thompson
kept.prior_reasoning: Thompson's emphasis on diversion and the harm of incarceration ("jailing disrupts lives") signals a skeptical posture toward pretrial detention, consistent with stance 2: hold prosecution to strict standards on detention requests.

kept.name: Zachary Smith
kept.prior_reasoning: Smith criticizes wealth-based detention and says the standard should be "the least restrictive way to ensure the defendant's return to court." He explicitly rejects cash bail as a proxy for flight risk, consistent with skepticism toward prosecution-driven detention requests.

kept.name: Aida Ashouri
kept.prior_reasoning: Ashouri has direct, specific positions on police accountability. Her Patch Q&A states: "As city attorney, I would reform the criminal division and train attorneys to recognize cases where constitutional rights are violated and to not file those cases. My goal would be to abolish racial profiling in my office. This will also impact the LAPD as they will be disincentivized to arrest when they knew that we would not file those cases." The LAist voter guide confirms she described "how overpolicing leads to racial profiling and the criminalization of poverty." Her platform explicitly commits to "protecting our rights to protest and be free from unreasonable search and seizure." The SPNA DTLA article summarizes: "Police Accountability: Emphasizes protecting the right to protest and freedom from unreasonable search and seizure." Her approach — using prosecutorial declination as an accountability mechanism against LAPD, abolishing racial profiling, declining unconstitutional cases — maps directly to value 1: the office investigates independently and works for the public, not for officials it is supposed to keep accountable.

kept.name: Andrea Joy Campbell
kept.prior_reasoning: Campbell proposed a police oversight board in 2020 as a Boston City Councilor and passed an ordinance limiting crowd control weapons (2021). She also refused to advance $1.2M in BPD grants in 2021 in her public safety committee chair role over accountability concerns. As AG she campaigned on ending qualified immunity and creating a Police Accountability Unit within the AG's Office (though she moderated her qualified immunity position after taking office). She challenged biased police promotion exams and criticized the BPD union's conduct.

kept.name: Brooke Jenkins
kept.prior_reasoning: Jenkins' office maintains an Independent Investigations Bureau tracking officer-involved shootings and in-custody deaths, and her office has pursued some accountability cases. However, she has strongly supported police cooperation and expanded surveillance (Prop E, 2022). Public defenders alleged her office withheld evidence at least 50 times between September 2024 and February 2025, including body camera footage — suggesting limited enthusiasm for transparency that disadvantages prosecution.

kept.name: David Chiu
kept.prior_reasoning: No direct bills specifically on police accountability were found in Chiu's legislative record, but his consistent civil rights legislation (corporate diversity mandates, immigrant protections, fair chance licensing) indicates support for ensuring police accountability. His City Attorney role involves oversight of city legal matters including police department legal exposure. Insufficient specific evidence — assigning based on legislative pattern.

kept.name: Dawn McIntosh
kept.prior_reasoning: Described a data-driven claims approach in which her office reviews claims and lawsuits to spot trends and works with departments to fix underlying problems, representing the city while acknowledging and addressing meritorious systemic issues.

kept.name: Heather Ferbert

Her office prosecutes officer misconduct cases referred by the Commission. She supports civilian oversight infrastructure while maintaining strong prosecution of violent crime.

kept.name: Hydee Feldstein Soto
kept.prior_reasoning: Has a mixed record on police accountability. A judge found evidence of biased prosecution in her decision to charge 31 pro-Palestine protesters for blocking traffic, with internal memos showing she expressed inordinate interest in the investigation and suggested specific individuals for prosecution to LAPD. Moderate overall on accountability.

kept.name: Jay Jones
kept.prior_reasoning: Jones supported police reform legislation as a delegate, including measures related to use of force and chokeholds, and his 2021 justice reform plan included "improving policing and ending brutality and abuse." He advocated for the AG's office to prioritize civil rights enforcement against police misconduct. However, he simultaneously championed historic law enforcement funding increases and framed his public safety plan as developed in partnership with state and local law enforcement.

kept.name: Jeffrey S. Gray
kept.prior_reasoning: In February 2026 Gray independently found a 2024 Saratoga Springs officer-involved shooting 'not justified' and filed criminal charges (aggravated assault and reckless endangerment) against Officer Dean Sekona. He wrote that 'officer Sekona only fired his weapon after Valenzuela began to drive away — when any possible threat to the officers or others diminished' and concluded 'the answer is no' to whether probable cause for deadly force existed. This is a concrete accountability action. However, his professional background and campaign platform emphasized strong law-enforcement collaboration and he trains officers on Fourth Amendment doctrine in a pro-prosecution frame.

kept.name: John McKinney
kept.prior_reasoning: McKinney's approach to police misconduct litigation is grounded in vigorous litigation management and liability reduction, not independent accountability. His Patch Q&A states: "As city attorney, I would implement an aggressive risk management strategy to reduce lawsuits and payouts, vigorously defend against frivolous claims, and settle meritorious cases early to avoid costly verdicts." He frames this as knowing "which cases to fight and which to resolve" — a liability management lens. His primary critique of the incumbent is about the LAPD data breach as a management and transparency failure, not about failure to hold police accountable for misconduct. He is endorsed by the Los Angeles Police Protective League (LAPD officer union) and former DAs Nathan Hochman and Jackie Lacey, both with law-enforcement-aligned records. His platform contains no statement about independent investigation of police misconduct, civilian oversight support, or systemic LAPD accountability. The pattern — vigorous defense of city employees, settling meritorious claims to cut costs (not as an accountability mechanism), police union endorsement — most closely matches value 4: defend city employees vigorously; that is the job; settlements invite more lawsuits. He does not reach value 5 because he explicitly acknowledges settling meritorious cases rather than defending everything regardless of merit.

kept.name: Kent Davis
kept.prior_reasoning: Davis's campaign is built around 'supporting law enforcement' and he is endorsed by a Sheriff, the Utah Attorney General, and the former Governor. He has made no statement about independently investigating or prosecuting police misconduct. His framing positions law enforcement as partners in public safety, not as actors to be scrutinized. — best matches stance 4 (defend/support city employees vigorously; settlements invite more lawsuits).

kept.name: Marissa Roy
kept.prior_reasoning: Roy's approach to police misconduct liability combines accountability with smart settlement practice. The SPNA DTLA article identifies as a key platform element: "Critical of Incumbent: Her platform argues the current administration has spent too much on 'liability payouts' and has been overly aggressive in suing journalists and protesters." Her Patch Q&A states regarding legal liability: "For more long-term solutions, I'd work to bring departments in compliance with the law so that we prevent lawsuits before they occur" — framing LAPD compliance as a priority for reducing costs through accountability. The AOL/LA Times piece quotes her vowing "to put a particular focus on the Los Angeles Police Department, making sure it follows through on the recommendations drafted in the wake of costly litigation." Her proposed liability audit by City Controller Kenneth Mejia would scrutinize the office's existing settlement and defense practices for police-related cases. The LA Forward voter guide describes Roy as committed to "holding abusive police accountable" and contrasts her with the incumbent's posture of defending city departments against misconduct lawsuits. Roy's position — settle valid claims, make LAPD follow through on recommendations, audit existing practices — maps to value 2: settle valid claims quickly and pursue real accountability; defending misconduct wastes money and public trust. She does not reach value 1 (independent investigation against officials) because her emphasis is on smart liability management that produces accountability as a byproduct, not on the office acting as an independent police watchdog.

kept.name: Nathan Hochman
kept.prior_reasoning: Hired an independent special prosecutor specifically to handle cases of law enforcement misconduct, framing the DA office as working for the public rather than for law enforcement. Has stated the office will prosecute officers when evidence warrants. Aligns with answer [1]: investigate independently; the office works for the public, not the officials it is supposed to hold accountable.

kept.name: Rob Bonta
kept.prior_reasoning: As California AG, Bonta leads implementation of AB 1506 (signed 2020), which mandates independent DOJ review of all officer-involved shootings resulting in unarmed civilian deaths and requires public reports with policy recommendations. He launched a Police Practices Review Division in 2023 and has investigated multiple departments including San Bernardino County, San Luis Obispo, San Joaquin County, and LAPD. His approach involves strong civilian oversight through independent investigation while prioritizing reform-focused recommendations alongside accountability rather than abolition.

kept.name: Shawn Robinson
kept.prior_reasoning: Robinson's two decades as public defender — representing defendants against the state — and his campaign emphasis on "accountability and fairness" suggest he would settle valid claims against police misconduct and pursue real accountability rather than reflexively defending law enforcement. He has no direct statements on prosecuting officers specifically, but the public defender orientation is the strongest available signal.

kept.name: Sim Gill
kept.prior_reasoning: Gill released 22 proposed changes to Utah's deadly force laws in 2020, calling current law 'more generous to law enforcement officers than to other members of our community,' and stated 'if we want different outcomes, we need different laws.' However, in practice he rarely charged officers — it took until May 2026 for him to charge a police officer in a fatal shooting for the first time in over a decade, citing the high legal threshold required. His reform advocacy has focused on changing the law rather than prosecuting under existing standards.

kept.name: Aida Ashouri
kept.prior_reasoning: Ashouri consistently treats prosecution as a last resort, with treatment, mediation, and community services as preferred interventions. Her platform explicitly states "Housing over handcuffs" and focuses "on alternatives to incarceration." Her Patch Q&A describes dismissing cases where evidence was insufficient, allowing "changes in sentencing for non-violent cases to allow for people to seek rehabilitation," making a policy "not to criminalize poverty," and treating "substance abuse as a crime but a public health matter." Her platform commits to "prioritizing mediation and restorative justice" and restarting the Neighborhood Prosecutor program to "resolve issues without punitive measures." The AOL/LA Times piece quotes her: "We need to focus on cases that are harming people," implying prosecution reserved for genuine harm. She explicitly says "housing over handcuffs" and frames drug addiction as public health, not crime — maps directly to value 1: prosecution is a last resort; connecting people to treatment, housing, or job programs does more good than a criminal record.

kept.name: Andrea Joy Campbell
kept.prior_reasoning: Campbell pledged as AG to pursue gun violence, abortion-rights violations, elder fraud, police misconduct, housing discrimination, and corporate consumer fraud as prosecution priorities — all reflecting an equity-focused enforcement agenda. She created specific units for gun violence prevention, reproductive justice, elder justice, and police accountability. She has committed to ensuring powerful interests are not treated as "above the law" and has pursued corporate violations harming consumers alongside her social justice priorities.

kept.name: Brian Schwalb
kept.prior_reasoning: As AG Schwalb's office focuses on consumer protection, housing rights, worker rights, environmental protection, and civil rights enforcement using the office's resources to address systemic issues rather than maximizing prosecutorial caseload. Value=2 matches 'Use diversion when it is available and makes sense. Reserve prosecution for when community safety actually requires it.'

kept.name: Brooke Jenkins
kept.prior_reasoning: Jenkins made fentanyl and narcotics trafficking her top prosecution priority — announcing over 30 felony narcotics trafficking charges in a single month (November 2025), pursuing drug trafficking convictions in the Tenderloin and SOMA, and aggressively charging repeat offenders. She also enabled gang enhancements and adult prosecution of minors in a broader range of cases than her predecessor.

kept.name: Dan Patterson
kept.prior_reasoning: Patterson's office actively operates Treatment Court, DWI Court, Veterans Court, and a Restorative Justice Program for first-time non-violent offenders when appropriate, while simultaneously maintaining vigorous prosecution of serious and violent cases. The community safety unit manages adult treatment court alongside felony narcotics prosecution, and partners with the Community Alternative Sentencing Program (CASP). The office's stated approach is to use alternative sentencing 'when appropriate' as a judgment call, not as the default — aligning with stance 3.

kept.name: David Chiu
kept.prior_reasoning: As City Attorney (not DA), Chiu focuses on civil affirmative litigation and city representation rather than criminal prosecution. His office has pursued wage theft lawsuits, drug enforcement actions (Tenderloin corner store), and consumer protection cases. This mixed portfolio — worker protection alongside street-level drug enforcement — suggests balanced prosecution priorities that address both economic crimes and public safety.

kept.name: Doug Haubert
kept.prior_reasoning: Haubert is a national leader in court diversion who created PAD, LEAD, restorative justice and CSW programs for nonviolent/first-time offenders, while still prosecuting and enforcing the law when public safety requires (gangs, DV).

kept.name: Heather Ferbert
kept.prior_reasoning: The City Attorney's 2025-2026 enforcement actions document selective prosecution: fentanyl dealers, worker misclassification (Campbell's lawsuit Feb 2026), antitrust (fire truck manufacturers Apr 2026), illegal marijuana retailers (Apr 2026), and illegal massage parlors (May 2026). Ferbert also aggressively pursues consumer protection and environmental enforcement through the ACE Unit rather than a pure crime-focused or pure civil-rights-only approach.

kept.name: Hydee Feldstein Soto
kept.prior_reasoning: Focuses prosecution resources on sex trafficking (Western Avenue Initiative targeting sex buyers and traffickers), impaired driving, and sexual abuse cases — a progressive approach to prosecution priorities that targets exploitation and harm rather than low-level offenses.

kept.name: Ismael R. Ozanne
kept.prior_reasoning: Says top goal is preventing cases from reaching his office via safe diversion; does not charge standalone simple marijuana possession

kept.name: Jay Jones
kept.prior_reasoning: Jones's reform plan called for making the justice system "fairer and more equitable" and ending disparities that disadvantage people of color and those with lesser economic means. He proposed specialty dockets for mental health and addiction. kept.name: Jeffrey S. Gray
kept.prior_reasoning: Gray's enacted priorities are violent crime (Major Crimes Division), sexual assault (SVU doubled to 10 attorneys by 2025 with projected 406 filings), and death penalty cases. He said 'With SVU cases, these individuals, mostly men who assault women, deserve to go to prison' and acknowledged 'The reality is, the system would crash if we didn't have plea bargains' — using them instrumentally. He explicitly criticized pre-filing diversion as inappropriate and raised case filings substantially from his predecessor's reform-era levels.

kept.name: John McKinney
kept.prior_reasoning: McKinney's prosecution framework covers a broad set of cases requiring active prosecution: repeat offenders, retail theft, organized shoplifting, illegal firearms, street racing, open-air drug markets, and encampment-related quality-of-life crimes. His Patch Q&A states: "The focus of the Los Angeles City Attorney's Office must be on the crimes that are most directly impacting the public safety of our communities and the quality of life of our neighborhoods. That means prioritizing cases involving repeat offenders who drive quality-of-life crime through theft, vandalism, and destruction of property." His LAist campaign survey confirms he "will focus on repeat offenders driving down quality-of-life crime, retail theft and organized shoplifting, illegal firearms, and dangerous activities such as street racing and open-air drug markets." His "compassionate accountability" framing includes working with diversion programs and service providers, but explicitly as a complement to prosecution — he describes restoring order in public spaces as the primary goal, with services helping individuals "access housing, treatment and support" after enforcement contact. This positions him at value 4: prosecute all solid cases; declination requires a strong reason. He does not reach value 5 because he explicitly acknowledges diversion's role and describes his approach as "not about punishment for its own sake."

kept.name: Marissa Roy
kept.prior_reasoning: Roy's prosecution framework centers on diversion as the primary response to nonviolent misdemeanors, with prosecution reserved for cases that genuinely require it. Her Patch Q&A states: "Diversion is a tailored, court-supervised program that connects people with the services they need to address that cause, such as behavioral health treatment, addiction support and counseling. Data has shown that when nonviolent misdemeanors are addressed with diversion, rather than incarceration, people are dramatically less likely to reoffend." She describes her philosophy as "develop tools like diversion that are shown to work, collaborate with communities to develop sustainable, neighborhood-centered solutions, and work to permanently break cycles of criminalization." The AOL/LA Times piece quotes her directly: Roy "has promised to place a heavy emphasis on the legal process known as diversion… In cases involving nonviolent crimes, diversion is more likely than jail to keep people from becoming repeat offenders. 'It makes not only the person whole, but the community safer.'" At the same time, Roy does not call for abandoning prosecution entirely — her LAist candidate survey states she would use "the office's misdemeanor authority to prosecute ICE agents," and her Patch Q&A notes "That does not mean freezing misdemeanor prosecution — it means right-sizing and tailoring our approach based on what will most effectively serve public safety." This is precisely value 2: use diversion when available and appropriate; reserve prosecution for when community safety actually requires it.

kept.name: Nathan Hochman
kept.prior_reasoning: Immediately reversed Gascón's blanket misdemeanor non-filing policy; charged approximately 70% of low-level cases that his predecessor declined. Restored sentencing enhancements including three-strikes and gang enhancements. In practice, declination requires a strong affirmative reason. Aligns with answer [4]: prosecute all solid cases; declination is the exception.

kept.name: Rob Bonta
kept.prior_reasoning: As AG, Bonta pursues a balance of accountability and treatment-focused approaches. He expanded DOJ investigation of officer-involved shootings, championed opioid settlement funds for treatment, and supported Legal Services Corporation funding for civil legal aid. His legislative record includes reducing administrative fees on people in the criminal justice system and cannabis resentencing. He prosecutes serious crimes vigorously (organized crime, human trafficking, gun trafficking) while supporting alternatives to incarceration for non-violent offenders.

kept.name: Shawn Robinson
kept.prior_reasoning: Robinson's core campaign platform centers on "alternatives to incarceration" as a primary strategy, with prosecution reserved for when community safety actually requires it. His 20+ years as a public defender reinforces this orientation — he approaches the role as a reform-minded prosecutor who sees diversion and rehabilitation as preferred tools.

kept.name: Sim Gill
kept.prior_reasoning: Gill built Salt Lake County's County Pre-File Intervention Program (CPIP), diverting hundreds of low-level and non-violent cases before charges are filed, with a 3.4% recidivism rate among graduates. He has explicitly targeted diverting 10% of all case screenings into pre-filing diversion, especially for those experiencing mental health issues and homelessness. Stated goal: 'It is possible to invest in criminal justice reform without compromising on public safety.'
